flashcards.definition: The full-size memory module used in desktop PCs, offering higher capacities and better performance than laptop modules.
The smaller memory module used in laptops and other compact computers, with lower capacities than a desktop DIMM.
The family of system RAM that is synchronized to the system clock and moves data on both edges of each clock cycle; its generations include DDR3, DDR4, and DDR5.
The DDR generation just before DDR4, with modules of up to 16 GB.
The DDR generation after DDR3 that brought better power efficiency and higher density, with modules of up to 32 GB.
The newest DDR generation, which splits each module into two 32-bit subchannels and will not fit a DDR4 slot.
The system memory that running programs and open files load into; faster than SSDs and HDDs but volatile, so it holds data only while powered on.
Server and workstation memory that fixes single-bit errors and halts the system on multi-bit errors; the motherboard and CPU must both support it.
The ordinary memory in most consumer PCs, without the extra 8-bit checksum the memory controller uses to catch and fix errors.
A memory setup with one 64-bit data bus to the RAM, which can limit transfer rates; a PC may fall back to it when its modules do not match.
Two 64-bit pathways (128 bits per transfer) that double memory bandwidth, using identical ordinary modules in the matching slot of each channel, such as A1 and B1.
Three memory channels, supported by some CPUs and chipsets; with fewer modules installed, the system uses only as many channels as are filled.
Four memory channels, supported by some CPUs and chipsets; with fewer modules installed, the system uses only as many channels as are filled.
A mode for mismatched module sizes that runs the matching amount in dual-channel and the leftover memory in single-channel.
A drive that stores data on spinning metal or glass platters with a magnetic coating, using read/write heads on a moving actuator; most connect by SATA.
How fast an HDD's platters spin in revolutions per minute: 5,400 or 7,200 on average drives and 10,000 or 15,000 on high-performance drives.
The larger of the two main hard drive form factors, used for drives inside desktop PCs.
The smaller of the two main hard drive form factors, used in laptops and portable drives; an adapter caddy fits it in a 3.5-inch bay.
An internal drive that stores data in flash memory with no moving parts, so it reads much faster than an HDD and better withstands shock.
The SSD interface that runs directly over the PCIe bus for far more speed than SATA, on an expansion card or in an M.2 slot.
The drive interface used by most HDDs and by 2.5-inch SSDs; its 600 MBps limit can bottleneck fast SSDs.
The motherboard's standard bus for expansion cards, which fast NVMe SSDs also use directly for better performance.
An enterprise drive interface, faster and more reliable than SATA, that links many drives to one controller; common in servers and workstations.
A small SSD form factor that lies flat on the motherboard, draws power from its slot with no cable, and can use SATA or NVMe.
A small SATA-only SSD card that plugs into a combined data and power port on the motherboard.
The general way of combining several disks into one volume the OS sees as a single drive, for fault tolerance, speed, or both; its levels include 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10.
Striping without parity across at least two disks; it is faster, but if any disk fails, the whole volume is lost.
Mirroring on two disks; every write goes to both, so one disk can fail without data loss, but only half the space is usable.
Striping with parity spread across at least three disks; it survives one disk failure and gives up one disk's worth of space to parity.
Striping with two sets of parity across at least four disks; it survives two disks failing at once and gives up two disks' worth of space.
A stripe of mirrored pairs on at least four disks, always an even number; one disk in each mirror can fail, and half the space goes to mirroring.
A flash memory board with a built-in USB connector and protective cover that plugs into any USB port; also called a thumb drive or pen drive.
Removable flash storage, such as Secure Digital (SD), used in cameras, phones, and tablets; a PC needs a card reader to use it.
A drive that uses a laser to read and write CDs, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs; an internal one fits a 5.25-inch bay and connects by SATA.
The PSU's plugs that deliver DC power: the 24-pin P1 for the motherboard, 4/6/8/16-pin leads for the CPU and PCIe cards, SATA power, and Molex.
A CPU socket design with the pins in the motherboard socket and flat contact pads on the CPU; Intel's usual design, now used by AMD's newer sockets too.
A CPU socket design with the pins on the CPU, which fit into the motherboard socket; AMD's traditional design, as in AM4.
A motherboard with two or more CPU sockets for symmetric multiprocessing (SMP), each holding an identical CPU; used in servers and high-end workstations.
CPU features such as Intel VT or AMD-V that help virtual machines perform better; they may need to be enabled in BIOS/UEFI setup.
The processor, which executes the instruction code of firmware, the operating system, and applications.
The 32-bit CISC instruction set of Intel and AMD processors, which can address no more than 4 GB of RAM.
The 64-bit extension of x86, called AMD64 or Intel 64; it can use more than 4 GB of RAM and runs both 32-bit and 64-bit software.
A power-efficient RISC processor design, usually built as a system-on-chip, used in most Android devices and in Apple's M1 and M2 chips.
A CPU design using simpler instructions that usually finish in one clock cycle each, for better performance per watt; ARM is based on it.
A processor with two or more cores on a single chip, each with its own execution unit and cache; also called chip-level multiprocessing (CMP).
A CPU feature that lets each physical core run two threads at once (Intel calls it Hyper-Threading), so an eight-core CPU is listed as 8C/16T.
Move air through the case, drawing cool air in the front vents and pushing warm air out the back; thermometer sensors set their speed and detect failures.
A part that cools a chip by adding surface area; memory uses passive ones called heat spreaders, and CPUs use active ones that typically have a fan.
The material between a CPU and its heat sink that fills air gaps for efficient heat transfer; harder to apply than a thermal pad but may be more reliable.
A solid sheet between a chip and its heat sink that softens when heated; easier to apply than paste but may be less reliable.
Pumps coolant through water blocks and radiators, cooling better than air and often more quietly; all-in-one coolers are simpler closed loops for one CPU or GPU.
The lower AC input range, about 120 V, supplied by North American wall outlets.
The higher AC input range, 220 to 240 V, supplied by UK outlets and used by many data centers for efficiency.
A dual-voltage PSU that adjusts itself to low-line or high-line input, unlike a PSU with a manual switch that must be set to match the outlet.
The component that converts AC from the wall outlet into the low-voltage DC (3.3, 5, and 12 V) that PC parts use.
A PSU output wire that carries current at one DC voltage, such as +3.3, +5, or +12 V; the +12 V one is the most heavily used.
The PSU's main P1 cable to the motherboard: 24 pins, with 4 that come off so it also fits older 20-pin boards.
A second PSU that takes over at once if the first fails; standard in servers, where a failed unit can often be swapped without powering down.
A PSU with detachable cables, so only the needed ones are attached, cutting clutter and improving airflow and cooling.
The most power a PSU can output, in watts; it must cover all the components' combined needs, or the PC may shut down or reboot at random.
How much of the power a PSU draws from the outlet reaches the components as DC, with the rest lost as heat; shown by 80 PLUS ratings.
